1.pericope_label: The daughters of Zelophehad stand before Moses and ask a possession
debates: How the father’s name was to be preserved: the Targum of Jonathan, with which Jarchi agrees, makes the request a plea that their mother might marry their father’s brother under the levirate law, which Gill objects to on the ground that it does not appear the law was yet in being, while admitting he cannot easily say how else the name would be preserved; a second reading, which Gill reports and Wesley says some gather, is that the first son of each heiress was called after Zelophehad or after Hepher; a third, which Gill thinks confirmed by the context, is that the Jews commonly understand by the name no other thing than the inheritance itself

What the words about dying in his own sin exclude: Calvin holds that by denying their father was in the company of Korah they exclude the crimes whose punishment fell upon the posterity of the criminals, so that his private sin stands contrasted with public ignominy, and calls it mere childish nonsense for the Jews to affirm that Zelophehad was the sabbath wood-gatherer or one of those slain; Wesley takes the phrase at face value as meaning personal sins, and adds the Jewish belief behind it that death was a punishment for a man’s own sins

Whether female inheritance is rule or exception: Calvin holds that since the law gives no name to women it would seem no account of them was to be taken in the division, that God laid this down as the general rule, and that what follows is a special exception for the preservation of the name; and he concedes, as the others do not, that the point is open to dispute with obvious arguments both for and against it
outliers: Henry's description of the court in English terms, Moses sitting as king, the princes as lords, and the elders whom the people had chosen as their commons
Henry's supposition that the personal character of the women added weight to the plea, which is why the case is noticed so often

Calvin's generosity about the motive, that although the daughters plead for their own private advantage the discussion arose from a good principle, since they would never have been so anxious if God's promise had not been to them as certain as if they already held the land
Calvin's observation that the restriction of the plea in time aided their cause, since carrying the question back to an earlier period might have originated many quarrels
The editorial gloss supplying what Calvin refuses, that Jarchi reports Rabbi Akiba for the wood-gathering and Rabbi Simeon for the contumacious company
Wesley's note on the confidence of the request, that they asked a possession in a land not yet conquered, concluding it certainly would be, and thereby gave glory to God

5.pericope_label: Moses brings their cause before the Lord; the general law of inheritance
debates: Why the masculine pronoun is used of the daughters: Clarke insists on the anomaly, that the masculine forms stand where the feminine were to be expected though governed by the noun for daughters, and reports three explanations with visible reserve, remarking that interpreters have sought a hidden meaning here and have found several, whether hidden here or not — that the daughters are treated as if they were heirs male, that it is on account of their faith and regard to ancient custom, and that it signifies the free gift of God; Ellicott offers a fourth possibility Clarke does not report, that the reference may be to the sons of Zelophehad’s daughters

Why the cause went up to God: Gill takes it as jurisdiction, that the question was too difficult for the court and devolved on Moses as its president, and counts it with the Targums as one of four such causes; Calvin supposes rather that the judges were divided or in doubt, and holds it expedient that the rule be laid down by God so that no future controversy might arise, a human sentence perhaps not setting the obstinacy of many at rest

How far the preference for daughters reaches: Calvin holds that God prefers the daughters to all other relatives where there is no male issue, but that with this single exception at the first degree he admits none but males and so preserves the usual order, giving a reason on each side, that it would be very unjust to exclude a man’s own natural heirs for their sex, and that once it became necessary to pass beyond his own children the prerogative of the male line began
outliers: Gill's rabbinic frame, that the Targums count this one of four causes which came before Moses and which he solved according to the mind of the Lord, the others being the blasphemer, those defiled by the dead, and the sabbath breaker

Calvin's remark on the pious modesty of Moses, who was not ashamed to confess his ignorance until instructed by the mouth of God, and who, though he had promulgated the law forty years before, was still always ready to learn
Calvin's standing lesson that rulers ought to have recourse to God in points of perplexity even though he no longer delivers answers from heaven
Keil's setting out of the whole order of succession, son, then daughters, then brothers, then paternal uncles, then next of kin
The agreement of Keil and Ellicott in sending the reader to the same two authorities on the Hebrew law of succession, Keil's own antiquities and Selden's treatise
Calvin's express limitation of the whole discussion to the land of Canaan, in which the name of Abraham and the names of the twelve tribes were to be preserved
themes: brought their cause before the Lord
the prerogative of the male line

9.pericope_label: The rest of the succession; get thee up into mount Abarim and be gathered
debates: How Abarim, Nebo and Pisgah are related: Clarke identifies the mountain flatly as Nebo and takes Nebo to be the same as Pisgah; Wesley arranges the three differently, making Abarim the whole tract, Nebo one of its highest points, and Pisgah the top of Nebo; Ellicott arranges them differently again, making the mountains of Abarim the Moabitish table-land whose northern portion bore the name Pisgah, and observing that Nebo is sometimes described as one of the mountains of Abarim and at other times as the top of Pisgah

What it is to be gathered to one’s people: Ellicott rules out one reading, that in the case of Moses, as in that of Abraham, the expression cannot be understood with reference to the place of burial; Wesley supplies the positive sense, that death does not cut Moses off but gathers him to rest with the holy patriarchs, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob being his people, the people of his choice

Whether the statute’s brethren include sisters: Wesley enters a correction the text itself does not make, that where the statute says brethren sisters are to be understood as well, grounding it on the clause about daughters a few verses earlier, while Keil and Gill state the chain of succession as it stands
outliers: Ellicott's observation on the placing of the command, that it stands in immediate connection with the answer to the daughters of Zelophehad, so that those who were to inherit and the lawgiver who was to be excluded are set side by side, and that Moses does not shrink from recording his own sentence in that position

Henry's account of the fault, that Moses failed to express as carefully as he ought a regard to the honour both of God and of Israel, and that though highly favoured he shall hear of it and all the world shall hear of it too

Henry's warning that those in reputation for wisdom and honour have need to be constantly careful of their words and ways, lest they say or do what may be a diminution to their comfort or their credit a great while after
Clarke's citation of Dr Shaw, that the range is a long ridge of frightful, rocky, precipitous hills continued all along the eastern coast of the Dead Sea as far as the eye can reach
Clarke's etymology, that the name comes from the verb to pass over, so that Abarim probably signifies passages, the ridge being named from the passage of the Israelites opposite it
Gill's note that the seeing was all Moses was admitted to, entrance being denied him though he importuned for it

15.pericope_label: Moses prays for a successor; the God of the spirits of all flesh
debates: Why Moses asked rather than appointed: Calvin makes it humility about a competence he actually possessed, that it was permitted him to choose officers as part of the political constitution but that this task was too difficult for man’s judgment, so the power had to be entrusted to God alone; Ellicott makes it self-denial about a preference he might have indulged, that instead of appointing one of his own family or the man of his own choosing he commits the matter to God

What the phrase about going out and coming in covers: Gill offers three readings without choosing, that it means going before them in war and bringing them home in peace, or simply the administration of civil government, or something particular to leading Israel out of the wilderness into Canaan; Ellicott takes the first pair as a common idiom for the ordinary life of man and the second as the direction of the conduct of others; Wesley explains it from shepherding practice and Clarke from what it shows of Moses himself

What the title God of the spirits of all flesh stresses: Gill presses the second half, that the souls of men are so called precisely to distinguish embodied spirits from the angels, who though spirits are incorporeal; Wesley presses the first half and its consequence, that this is the searcher of spirits who knows who is fit, and the giver and governor of spirits who can raise and suit them to the highest and hardest works
outliers: Henry's sentence fixing the character of the prayer, that envious spirits do not love their successors and Moses was not one of these
Calvin's image for a people left without a leader, that they would remain like a headless body
Ellicott's making Moses a type of one greater, whose word was that they should weep not for him but for themselves and their children

The near-verbatim agreement of Wesley's comment with Henry's, that we should concern ourselves both in our prayers and in our endeavours for the rising generation, that God's kingdom may be advanced when we are in our graves
Keil's denial that the spirit in the next verse means insight and wisdom, making it instead the higher power inspired by God into the soul, which quickens the moral and religious life
Wesley's detail from shepherding practice, that shepherds in those countries did not walk behind their sheep as ours now do but before them, leading them out to pasture and in due time home again
themes: the God of the spirits of all flesh
go out and come in before them

18.pericope_label: Take thee Joshua, a man in whom is the spirit; put some of thine honour upon him
debates: What the spirit in Joshua is: Clarke will have it plainly that this must certainly mean the Spirit of God; Ellicott withholds that identification on grammatical grounds, noting that the definite article is not used in the original and that the word appears to denote spiritual endowment rather than the giver of it; Calvin agrees with Ellicott in substance and adds that the word is used here in a different sense from the sense it bore two verses earlier, standing by a common figure for the gifts that proceed from the Spirit; Wesley enumerates them as the spirit of government, of wisdom, and of the fear of the Lord

Whether the laying on of hands conferred anything or only declared it: Ellicott argues that it conferred, since the spiritual qualifications of Joshua did not supersede the necessity of an outward consecration and since a later text says Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom for Moses had laid his hands upon him; Wesley takes both together, that the ceremony designed the person and conferred the power; Gill sets a limit against exactly this, that what Moses was told to put upon Joshua was not the Spirit nor the gifts of the Spirit, since to do that is the Lord’s work and not any man’s, but the honour of civil government

What putting some of the honour upon him amounted to: Gill makes it a share in civil government, so that Joshua should be used no longer as a minister and servant but as colleague and partner, with some of the ensigns of power; Clarke reads it as public association, that Moses was to show the whole congregation he had associated Joshua with himself in the government; Wesley gives the reason of policy, that the people, being used to obey him while Moses lived, might do it afterwards the more cheerfully
outliers: Clarke's turn upon the ministry, that how miserably qualified is the man for the work of God who is not guided and influenced by the Holy Ghost, since God never chooses a man but one whom he has himself qualified
Calvin's list of the gifts the office needs, intelligence and judgment and magnanimity and skill in war
Calvin's notice of a fact he says is stated nowhere else, that Joshua was given in answer to the prayers of Moses
Calvin's note that the rite of laying on hands was in use before the giving of the Law, the holy patriarchs having blessed in this manner
Ellicott's supply of the words of the charge from a later chapter, that Joshua was to be strong and of a good courage
Gill's reason for the public setting, that the congregation might be witnesses of what was said and done and might receive and acknowledge him as having authority over them
themes: a man in whom is the spirit

21.pericope_label: He shall stand before Eleazar; Moses did as the Lord commanded him
debates: What Joshua’s standing before the priest signifies: Clarke takes it as a diminution and says so plainly, that here was a remarkable difference between him and Moses, since God talked with Moses face to face but spoke to Joshua only through the medium of the high priest; Calvin takes the same arrangement as a dignifying of the rule rather than a lowering of the ruler, since the prince consults God by the mouth of one who answers as the interpreter of God himself, and concludes that the passage shows the rule of Joshua was not profane

How constant the consulting was to be: Wesley limits it, that Joshua was to ask counsel when the case required it and in important and difficult matters; Ellicott states the obligation flatly, that Joshua and the children of Israel were to abide by the decision obtained through Urim and Thummim

What Moses’s obedience proves: Wesley argues that to ordain Eleazar and Joshua with his own hands while his own children were left common Levites was more to his glory than the highest advancement of his family, and shows a principle raising him above all other lawgivers, who always took care to establish their families; Gill puts the same facts to a different use, as clear proof that Moses was no impostor
outliers: Gill's rabbinic protocol, that the high priest did not stand before the king but the king before him, except that the king does not stand before him save when consulting by the judgment of Urim

Gill's notice that the posture here is not the ordinary one, since in consultation the priest faces the ark and the enquirer stands behind him facing the priest's back, whereas Joshua is described as standing before the priest

Calvin's conclusion from the arrangement, that in all legitimate dominion religion ought to hold the first place, and that it is absurd that things which depend wholly upon God should be separated from his service
Wesley's note that Urim is put for both Urim and Thummim
Jarchi's observation, reported by Gill, that Moses did the thing cheerfully and did more than he was commanded, since the Lord said lay thine hand and he laid both his hands

Clarke's suggestion that Peter alludes to this very circumstance, Joshua's receiving of the honour and glory of Moses, when he writes that Christ received from God the Father honour and glory, checked at once by his own remark that one infinitely greater than either Moses or Joshua is here
themes: at his word go out and come in
he laid his hands upon him
